question: Large non-EU e-commerce platforms such as Temu and Shein are increasingly penetrating the EU market by offering extremely low-cost goods, while often benefiting from loopholes in EU customs and product safety frameworks.

Independent testing and investigations across Member States (including Poland, Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary) report very high non-compliance rates for toys and consumer products sold via these online marketplaces.

This situation is particularly harmful for European small and medium enterprises, many of them based in central and eastern Europe, which cannot compete with the pricing and marketing power of such platforms.

While we welcome the Commission’s communication on e-commerce earlier this year, as well as its ongoing proceedings under the Digital Services Act and Consumer protection cooperation regulation against both Temu and Shein, these actions are progressing at a concerningly slow pace. In the light of this situation: 1.
When does the Commission expect to conclude these proceedings?
Does it agree that a stronger and more rapid response is urgently needed to defend the single market?
Will it deepen cooperation with Parliament and European businesses to tackle the issues set out above?
answer: The Commission is working at full speed on Digital Services Act (DSA) investigations (e.g. Temu, AliExpress, Shein) to reach swift yet legally sound conclusions on the cases. If the investigations confirm the existence of systemic risks on the platform, the Commission could adopt non-compliance decisions and ultimately impose fines or accept binding commitments.

The Commission also coordinates ongoing enforcement actions by the Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network against Temu and SHEIN (1) in response to identified consumer law infringements. To make the current consumer enforcement framework more effective and more deterrent, the Commission plans to propose a revision of the CPC Regulation during the 4th quarter of 2026 (2).

The Commission continues the implementation of the eCommerce Communication with results of the first product safety sweep and the Priority Control Area expected to contribute to a more robust enforcement framework, as will the use of EU IT tools, targeted enforcement via joint actions, and new EU testing facilities.

The upcoming EU Customs Reform, in final stage of negotiation, is expected to be adopted in 2026 to structurally reinforce the capabilities of EU customs and other enforcement authorities on e-commerce imports directly shipped to consumers.
The EU Market Surveillance Regulation is planned to be revised as part of the European Product Act legislative package, aiming to ensure level-playing field for businesses and safety for consumers.

The Commission will continue providing the Parliament with regular updates during the Committee on the internal market and Consumer Protection meetings to discuss the relevant Commission's services’ progress on online marketplaces regulation.

Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2017 on cooperation between national authorities responsible for the enforcement of consumer protection laws and repealing Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004, OJ L 345, 27 December 2017, pp. 1-26.

Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions — 2030 Consumer Agenda and action plan for consumers in the single market ‘A new impulse for consumer protection, competitiveness and sustainable growth’, COM/2025/848 final.
